# Public `swage.segment_reduce` on RTX A6000 at `c6099ec`

This record times the public `swage.segment_reduce` call on one NVIDIA RTX A6000
(`sm_86`) at revision `c6099ec56608faa636f44fb32d29ab475855e95f`, with a new offsets layout on every
call, beside `torch.segment_reduce` and looped Triton kernels. It holds
five runs, each repeated in five independent processes: one run of
rank-one values and four runs of `[N, D]` values.

It is the baseline for a planned change to the schedule of rank-two values.
That change is not part of this revision. Every `[N, D]` row here runs the
column kernel that the call launches at `c6099ec`, which
[The column kernel at this revision](#the-column-kernel-at-this-revision)
describes. A record of the same harness after the change is meant to be
compared with this one.

These are research measurements, not a performance gate. The machine was not
idle while they were taken; [Machine and conditions](#machine-and-conditions)
says what ran.

## What was measured

`benchmarks/benchmark_fresh_offsets.py` gives every iteration an offsets
layout that no earlier iteration used. The timed region of every candidate
runs from offsets in to result out. The runs differ in rank, size, widths,
and distributions, as their commands above state. Every run shares these
facts, quoted from the records:

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| Seed | 7 |
| Layout seeds | seed plus the iteration index, warmups first |
| Layout reuse | none; every iteration takes the next unused layout |
| Warmup layouts per row | 5 |
| Timed layouts per row | 100 |
| Warm step | before each sample, 2 untimed calls of the same candidate on the row's warm layout, each followed by a synchronize; the warm layout has its own seed and its own output buffer and is never timed or checked |
| Kinds | sum |
| Type | float32 |
| Values | CPU seeded randint(1, 8) / 4, float32, never zero; one buffer per row, filled row-major for [N, D] values, each layout reads its prefix |
| Pipeline | one call per sample, from an idle device |
| Candidate order | a new random permutation every iteration, shuffled by random.Random(order\_seed) with order\_seed '\<seed\>:\<distribution\>:\<iteration\>'; the seed and the order are recorded with each iteration |
| Clock | time.perf\_counter\_ns between two device synchronizations |
| Correctness | every candidate in every iteration, warmups included, against a float64 CPU torch.segment\_reduce reference along axis 0: a maximum and a minimum exactly; a sum exactly where sums of the values are exact in any order, otherwise within gamma(n - 1) times the sum of magnitudes in the unit of the dtype, doubled for float64, whose reference rounds too; a mean within that bound divided by n plus two units of its magnitude. An empty segment must give the reference value, infinite for a maximum or a minimum and NaN for a mean. Outputs start as NaN, or as 1e30 for a mean, and an output that still holds that value fails. Each row counts its exact, bounded, and unchecked results; for [N, D] values a result is one column of one segment |
| `[N, D]` rows | [N, D] rows time the public call on int32 and int64 offsets, torch.segment\_reduce along axis 0, and the looped rank-two Triton kernel, whose column block is the power of two from 4 to 64 that covers D best; each row records its block and block count. A row is admitted when its worst case holds at most 268435456 values. Its reference stays on the host, and every result is copied there to be checked |

The candidates that the runs timed, as the records describe them:

| Candidate | Surface | Entry point | Covers |
|---|---|---|---|
| `swage_cta_call` | private | swage.\_segmented\_qualification.launch\_gpu(values, offsets, out, 'sum'); not a call a user makes | sum; [N]; float32 |
| `swage_mixed` | private | swage.\_segmented\_qualification.\_prepare\_planned\_sum(values, offsets, out, warp\_max\_elements=32).mixed(); not a call a user makes | sum; [N]; float32 |
| `swage_public_call` | public | swage.segment\_reduce(values, offsets, kind, out=out) | sum, max, min, and mean; [N] and [N, D]; float32 and float64 |
| `swage_public_call_int64` | public | swage.segment\_reduce(values, offsets\_int64, kind, out=out) | sum, max, min, and mean; [N] and [N, D]; float32 and float64 |
| `torch` | baseline | torch.segment\_reduce(values, kind, offsets=offsets, axis=0) | sum, max, min, and mean; [N] and [N, D]; float32 and float64 |
| `triton_looped` | baseline | hand-written Triton, one looping program per segment | sum; [N]; float32 |
| `triton_planned` | baseline | hand-written Triton, packed short tasks and one block per longer task, partitioned on the device in the timed call | sum; [N]; float32 |
| `triton_planned_looped` | baseline | hand-written Triton, packed short tasks and looping longer tasks, partitioned on the device in the timed call | sum; [N]; float32 |
| `triton_rows_looped` | baseline | hand-written Triton, one program per segment and block of columns, looping over the rows | sum, max, min, and mean; [N, D]; float32 and float64 |

What the timed region of each covers:

| Candidate | Timed region |
|---|---|
| `swage_cta_call` | one launch\_gpu call (offset validation and transfer to the host, then one launch of the pure CTA kernel, which walks each segment in 128-thread blocks), then synchronize; no classification and no task upload |
| `swage_mixed` | \_prepare\_planned\_sum (offset validation and transfer to the host, classification, whatever kernel compilation and module loading the preparation path performs at this revision, task upload), then the mixed launch and synchronize |
| `swage_public_call` | one swage.segment\_reduce call with out= (the argument checks, offset validation and transfer to the host, classification, schedule selection, whatever kernel compilation and module loading the call performs at this revision, task upload, and the launches of the selected schedule), then synchronize |
| `swage_public_call_int64` | swage\_public\_call with int64 offsets, which are uploaded with the layout and outside the timer: the same call, with the validation of the int64 host copy, its narrowing to int32, and the upload of the private int32 copy the kernels read |
| `torch` | torch.segment\_reduce on the device offsets with its output allocation, along axis 0 for [N, D] values, then synchronize |
| `triton_looped` | one launch of the looped kernel, then synchronize; it needs no host classification |
| `triton_planned` | the partition (two torch.nonzero calls over the segment lengths on the device, each waiting for the device, and the conversion of the ids to int32), then the packed launch of the short tasks, one launch that reads one block of 4096 elements per longer task, then synchronize |
| `triton_planned_looped` | the partition (two torch.nonzero calls over the segment lengths on the device, each waiting for the device, and the conversion of the ids to int32), then the packed launch of the short tasks, one launch whose longer tasks loop over their segment in fixed blocks, then synchronize |
| `triton_rows_looped` | one launch of the looped rank-two kernel, one program per segment and block of columns, each walking the rows of its segment in fixed blocks, then synchronize; it needs no host classification |

The looped Triton candidates are swept: `triton_looped` over 15 block and
warp configurations for rank-one values, and `triton_rows_looped` over 5
configurations of rows per step and warps for `[N, D]` values. The rank-one
run also timed the private Swage candidates `swage_mixed` and
`swage_cta_call` and the planned Triton candidates. The tables below list
the private Swage candidates; the planned Triton candidates are in the
summaries and are not tabulated here.

## How the tables are built

- Every process contributes the median of its own samples. A cell in
  microseconds is the median of the five per-process medians.
- A ratio is formed inside each process from its two medians. A ratio cell
  gives the median of the five ratios and, in brackets, their minimum and
  maximum. Ratios to torch are the ones the summaries hold. The other
  ratios are formed by the same rule from the per-process medians in the
  summaries.
- A range in a statement or in the table of ranges runs from the lowest to
  the highest median ratio over the rows of a run.
- Microseconds are rounded to one decimal and ratios to two.
- A row is named as the summaries name it: the distribution, then `D=`
  and the width for `[N, D]` values.
- The best looped Triton configuration is the one with the lowest median
  in that row. It is chosen after the run from a sweep, separately for
  every row, so it is an optimistic bound for a Triton user who must pick
  one configuration in advance.

## Results

`swage.segment_reduce` (`swage_public_call`) against `torch.segment_reduce`, with a new offsets layout on every call. Each figure is the median across processes of the ratio of the two per-process medians, and the range is over the rows of the run:

- Rank one, 8,192 segments: 1.70 to 4.43 times as long, lowest on `uniform` and highest on `log-normal`; slower in every process in every one of the 9 rows.
- Rank two, 2,048 segments, D of 3 and 64: 1.57 to 4.82 times as long, lowest on `bimodal D=3` and highest on `many-tiny D=3`; slower in every process in every one of the 12 rows.
- Rank two, 8,192 segments, D of 3 and 64: 1.54 to 5.48 times as long, lowest on `bimodal D=64` and highest on `many-tiny D=3`; slower in every process in every one of the 12 rows.
- Rank two, 32,768 segments, D of 3 and 64: 1.38 to 7.66 times as long, lowest on `many-tiny D=64` and highest on `many-tiny D=3`; slower in every process in every one of the 8 rows.
- Rank two, 2,048 segments, D of 768: 1.50 to 17.06 times as long, lowest on `many-tiny D=768` and highest on `power-law D=768`; slower in every process in every one of the 4 rows.

On int64 offsets (`swage_public_call_int64`) the call took 0.99 to 1.57 times as long as on the int32 offsets of the same layouts, over all 45 rows.

The best looped Triton configuration of each row, chosen after the run, against `torch.segment_reduce`. A looped kernel has no planner: one program per segment, and per block of columns for `[N, D]` values, walks its segment in fixed blocks:

- Rank one, 8,192 segments: 0.63 to 0.98 times as long; the median is at or below one in every one of the 9 rows.
- Rank two, 2,048 segments, D of 3 and 64: 0.05 to 1.08 times as long; the median is at or below one in 11 of the 12 rows.
- Rank two, 8,192 segments, D of 3 and 64: 0.03 to 1.20 times as long; the median is at or below one in 10 of the 12 rows.
- Rank two, 32,768 segments, D of 3 and 64: 0.02 to 2.07 times as long; the median is at or below one in 6 of the 8 rows.
- Rank two, 2,048 segments, D of 768: 0.33 to 1.01 times as long; the median is at or below one in 3 of the 4 rows.

`swage_public_call` took 1.39 to 78.94 times as long as the best looped configuration of the row, and longer in every process in every one of the 45 rows.

## The column kernel at this revision

Every `[N, D]` row above runs one kernel, `segmented_sum_r2`, for both the
int32 and the int64 offsets. The processes of the four rank-two runs loaded
one PTX module of it, which their summaries list under `code.loaded_ptx`:

| File | Kernel | Bytes | SHA-256 | Loaded in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `segmented_sum_r2.ptx` | `segmented_sum_r2` | 2,275 | `ff8379311c4215bb5d34b195219a9cc69ef7fbe7f0b5aa57f6f466b22eca1131` | `public-r2-2048`, `public-r2-8192`, `public-r2-32768`, `public-r2-768-2048` |

`segmented_sum_r2.ptx` in the record directory is that module. It was
written again from the native build at this revision with
`python -m swage.compile --target sm_86`, which names it
`segmented_sum_r2.column.ptx`, and `public_call_tables.py --check` verifies
that its SHA-256 and size are the ones the summaries list. It was assembled
and disassembled with the CUDA 12.3 toolkit installed on the measuring
machine (`ptxas` release 12.3, V12.3.52):

```sh
cd benchmarks/results/segment-reduce-a6000-sm86-c6099ec
/usr/local/cuda/bin/ptxas -v -arch=sm_86 -o segmented_sum_r2.cubin segmented_sum_r2.ptx
/usr/local/cuda/bin/cuobjdump -sass segmented_sum_r2.cubin
```

The first command writes `segmented_sum_r2.cubin` beside the PTX. Do not
commit it. `ptxas -v` reported:

```text
ptxas info    : 0 bytes gmem
ptxas info    : Compiling entry function 'segmented_sum_r2' for 'sm_86'
ptxas info    : Function properties for segmented_sum_r2
    0 bytes stack frame, 0 bytes spill stores, 0 bytes spill loads
ptxas info    : Used 24 registers, 388 bytes cmem[0]
```

What the PTX and the SASS show:

- Threads per segment. The kernel requires blocks of 128 threads
  (`.reqntid 128, 1, 1`), and the call launches one block per segment, a
  grid of the segment count (`_launch_columns` in
  `python/swage/_segmented_qualification.py`, which `swage.segment_reduce`
  calls for `[N, D]` values with D other than 1). Each thread reads the two
  offsets of its segment and clamps them to the row count. Thread `t`
  reduces column `t`, then column `t + 128`, and so on while the column is
  below D. A thread with `t` at or above D exits before it reads a value.
  With D of 3, 3 threads of each block reduce a column; with D of 64, 64
  threads; with D of 768, all 128 threads, 6 columns each.
- Loop structure. A thread runs two nested loops. The outer loop steps over
  its columns by 128 and writes each result with one `STG.E`. The inner
  loop walks the rows of the segment for one column, one row per
  iteration, and was not unrolled. In the SASS that the commands above
  print, it runs from offset `0x02d0` to `0x0370`: eleven instructions.
  Two moves form the address, one `LDG.E` loads a 32-bit value, four
  instructions advance the 64-bit row index by D and the address by D
  times 4 bytes, two compare the index with the end of the segment, one
  `FADD` adds the value to the accumulator register, and one branch closes
  the loop. The `FADD` that consumes the load comes before the branch
  back, so a thread issues the next load of the loop after that `FADD`.
- Registers and memory. 24 registers per thread, no stack frame, and no
  spills. 388 bytes of constant bank 0, whose last 36 bytes, from offset
  0x160, are the six kernel parameters. No shared memory: the PTX declares
  no `.shared` variable, and the SASS has no shared-memory load or store,
  no barrier, and no shuffle.

This SASS is the output of `ptxas` 12.3, not the code the device ran. The
processes loaded the PTX through the CUDA driver, which compiles it for the
device itself (the machine table gives the driver and its API version).
That SASS was not dumped, and it can differ from the output above.

## What the record does not support

- A statement about the planned rank-two schedule. It is not part of this
  revision, and nothing here measures it.
- A statement about another GPU or architecture. One NVIDIA RTX A6000 (`sm_86`)
  ran everything.
- A statement about other seeds. Every row uses seed 7; the layouts
  of a row differ by iteration.
- A statement about other kinds, types, or rank-one sizes. Every row is a
  float32 sum, and the rank-one run has one size.
- A statement about calls in flight. Every sample is one call from an idle
  device.
- A statement about a quiet machine. Other development work ran on the CPU,
  and the CPU frequency governor was `powersave` throughout.
- A ranking of Triton configurations that a user could pick in advance.
  Every best configuration is chosen after the run.
- A gate. No threshold was declared before the run.

## Reproduce

With the native build, CUDA-enabled PyTorch, and Triton available, from a
clean worktree, and with `OUT` set to a new directory outside the checkout:

```sh
export PYTHONPATH="$PWD/python:$PWD/build/python_packages"
export SWAGE_CACHE_DIR="$OUT/cache"
python benchmarks/benchmark_processes.py --processes 5 --output-dir "$OUT/public-r1-8192" \
  -- benchmarks/benchmark_fresh_offsets.py --segment-count 8192 --exclude-candidates torch_pad_to_max
python benchmarks/benchmark_processes.py --processes 5 --output-dir "$OUT/public-r2-2048" \
  -- benchmarks/benchmark_fresh_offsets.py --segment-count 2048 --features 3 64 --distributions bimodal few-huge many-tiny one-outlier alternating-empty power-law
python benchmarks/benchmark_processes.py --processes 5 --output-dir "$OUT/public-r2-8192" \
  -- benchmarks/benchmark_fresh_offsets.py --segment-count 8192 --features 3 64 --distributions bimodal few-huge many-tiny one-outlier alternating-empty power-law
python benchmarks/benchmark_processes.py --processes 5 --output-dir "$OUT/public-r2-32768" \
  -- benchmarks/benchmark_fresh_offsets.py --segment-count 32768 --features 3 64 --distributions many-tiny one-outlier alternating-empty power-law
python benchmarks/benchmark_processes.py --processes 5 --output-dir "$OUT/public-r2-768-2048" \
  -- benchmarks/benchmark_fresh_offsets.py --segment-count 2048 --features 768 --distributions many-tiny one-outlier alternating-empty power-law
```

The campaign ran each command under `flock /tmp/swage-gpu.lock`, with the
compiled-kernel cache in a new directory. A rerun is a new measurement. Do
not write it into `benchmarks/results/`.

To regenerate this page and the documentation fragments from the committed
summaries, and to check them, the digests of the compressed process
records, and the committed PTX:

```sh
python benchmarks/public_call_tables.py
python benchmarks/public_call_tables.py --check
```
